notes.b: Before food can be absorbed it has to be broken down in two ways. Mechanical breakdown makes the pieces smaller; chemical breakdown then splits the molecules themselves. This subsection is about the first kind.
points: Mechanical (physical) digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, or fat into smaller droplets, without changing the molecules: no chemical bonds are broken and no new substances are formed. Chemical digestion, done by enzymes (biological catalysts that speed up reactions), does break bonds. There is more on this in Chemical breakdown.
Smaller pieces have a much larger total surface area, so enzymes can act on more of the food at once and digestion is faster. Think of how sugar dissolves faster as powder than as a lump.
Mechanical breakdown also makes food soft and moist enough to swallow, and mixes it with digestive juices (the watery secretions that contain enzymes), so the enzymes reach all of the food.
The four mechanisms are chewing by the teeth (mouth), peristalsis (the whole gut), churning (stomach), and emulsification of fats by bile salts (duodenum, the first part of the small intestine).
notes.tip: To distinguish mechanical from chemical digestion, say that mechanical digestion changes the size of the pieces while the molecules stay the same, whereas chemical digestion uses enzymes to break bonds.

notes.b: Digestion starts in the mouth, where the teeth cut and crush food into small pieces. Each type of tooth has a shape that suits its job.
points: Chewing (mastication) breaks food into small pieces and mixes it with saliva. The tongue rolls the moistened food into a bolus (a soft ball of food) for swallowing, and mucus in saliva lubricates the bolus so it slides down easily.
Incisors are at the front of the mouth. They are chisel-shaped with sharp, flat edges, which suits them for biting and cutting food.
Canines, one on each side of the incisors in each jaw, are pointed, so they grip and tear food. Human canines are small compared with those of carnivores (meat-eating animals).
Premolars and molars at the back are broad with ridged surfaces (cusps), for crushing and grinding food. Premolars have two cusps; molars are larger with more cusps.
The jaw moves sideways as well as up and down, so the broad surfaces of the molars can grind food rather than only crush it.

Diagram: (a) the four types of teeth side by side, labelled incisor, canine, premolar and molar, with their roles; (b) a vertical section of a molar labelled crown, root, enamel, dentine, pulp cavity, nerves and blood vessels, gum, cement and jawbone.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to state the function of each tooth type: incisors cut, canines grip and tear, premolars and molars crush and grind. For canines, make the one comparison that human canines are small compared with a carnivore's, and do not bring in other animals.

notes.b: The teeth in your mouth can be summarised in a short code called the dental formula. Knowing how a tooth is built also shows why it is hard-wearing yet sensitive.
points: The dental formula gives the number of each type of tooth in one half of the upper jaw over one half of the lower jaw, in the order incisors, canines, premolars, molars.
The adult human dental formula is 2.1.2.3 over 2.1.2.3, so there are 16 teeth on each side of the mouth (8 in each quarter) and 32 teeth in total.
Child's milk (deciduous) teeth have the formula 2.1.0.2 over 2.1.0.2, giving 20 teeth in total. They have no premolars, which is why the adult set has more teeth.
The third molars are the wisdom teeth. They appear last, often in the late teens or later, or not at all.
A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root fixed in the jawbone. Enamel, the hardest substance in the body, covers the crown, so it can withstand biting and chewing.
Dentine, a bone-like layer, lies beneath the enamel. The pulp cavity in the centre contains nerves and blood vessels, which is why a damaged tooth hurts. Cement holds the root in its socket.
notes.tip: The formula counts one side of the mouth only, upper over lower, so multiply by 2 to get the total of 32 (or 20 for milk teeth). Write the adult formula as 2.1.2.3 over 2.1.2.3.

notes.b: Enamel is very hard, but acid can still dissolve it. Tooth decay is the result of bacteria turning the sugar in the mouth into acid.
points: Bacteria in plaque (a sticky film on the teeth) feed on sugars and release acid. The acid dissolves enamel and then dentine, forming a cavity.
Eating and drinking sugary food less often gives the bacteria less to feed on, so less acid is made.

Brushing with fluoride toothpaste removes plaque and hardens enamel. Drinking fluoridated water (water with fluoride added) also hardens enamel, so it resists the acid. There is more on fluoride in Minerals.
Regular dental check-ups let decay be found and treated early, before the cavity reaches the pulp cavity.

notes.b: Food has to travel the whole length of the gut, even though the gut has no hands or pump. Peristalsis does this with waves of muscle, and it also helps break the food up.
points: Peristalsis is a wave of muscular contraction that passes along the wall of the gut, pushing food along. It happens from the oesophagus (the food pipe) to the rectum, and also in the ureters (the tubes from the kidneys to the bladder).
The gut wall has an inner layer of circular muscle and an outer layer of longitudinal muscle. Both are smooth, involuntary muscle, which means they work without conscious control.
1. The circular muscle just behind the bolus contracts, narrowing the gut and squeezing the food forwards.
2. The circular muscle just in front of the bolus relaxes, widening the gut to receive it. The wave then moves along, carrying the food with it.
Peristalsis is automatic (involuntary) once food is swallowed, and it works against gravity: a person can swallow while lying down or upside down, and the food still reaches the stomach.
Peristalsis also mixes food with digestive juices and breaks it up, so it is part of mechanical breakdown. In the small intestine it keeps moving the contents past the absorbing surface.
Dietary fibre adds bulk that the muscles can grip and push against, so a high-fibre diet keeps peristalsis effective and prevents constipation. There is more on this in Diet.

Diagram: a section of the gut showing a bolus with contracted circular muscle (narrow) behind it and relaxed muscle (wide) in front, with an arrow for the direction of movement; label circular muscle, longitudinal muscle, bolus, contraction and relaxation.
notes.tip: If asked to name the method that moves food along the alimentary canal, answer peristalsis. To explain how a high-fibre (wholegrain) diet helps, say that fibre adds bulk for the muscles to push against, so it keeps peristalsis working and prevents constipation. Peristalsis is not swallowing: swallowing starts it.

notes.b: The stomach is a muscular bag that holds food for a few hours. Its walls churn the food, which is the third mechanical process after chewing and peristalsis.
points: The stomach wall has three layers of smooth muscle: longitudinal, circular and an oblique (diagonal) layer. Having muscle running in three directions means their contractions churn the food, breaking it up and mixing it thoroughly with gastric juice (the stomach's digestive secretion).

After a few hours of churning, food becomes chyme, a thick, creamy liquid. The sphincters (rings of muscle that close an opening) at the entrance and exit stay closed during churning, so food is held in the stomach.

The pyloric sphincter, at the exit of the stomach, relaxes now and then to let small amounts of chyme into the duodenum. This means the small intestine is never overloaded and has time to digest and neutralise each portion.
The stomach also has a chemical role, using acid and pepsin. There is more on this in Chemical breakdown.
notes.tip: When describing churning, name the three muscle layers, including the oblique layer, and say that the contractions break food up and mix it with gastric juice.

notes.b: Fat is the hardest food to digest, because it does not mix with water. Bile salts solve this by breaking fat into tiny droplets, a mechanical step that gives the fat-digesting enzyme far more surface to work on.
points: Fats and oils do not mix with the watery contents of the gut, so they form large droplets. Lipase (the fat-digesting enzyme, which works in water) can therefore reach only the droplet surfaces.
Bile salts are made by the liver and enter the duodenum in bile. Each bile-salt molecule has one end that attracts water (hydrophilic) and one end that attracts fat (hydrophobic).

The bile salts gather on the surface of fat droplets with the fat-loving end inwards. With the churning of the gut they break the large droplets into many tiny droplets and stop them joining together again.
This is emulsification, and the mixture of tiny droplets in water is an emulsion.
Emulsification is mechanical: the fat molecules are unchanged and no bonds are broken. It greatly increases the surface area of fat exposed to lipase, so fat is digested much faster.
Bile contains no enzymes. Its other roles, neutralising stomach acid and excreting bile pigments (waste products), are in Chemical breakdown.
Washing-up liquid emulsifies grease in the same way, which is why bile salts are often compared to a detergent.
Diagram: one large fat droplet, then, after bile salts, many small droplets each coated with bile-salt molecules, labelled large surface area for lipase.
notes.tip: To state the role of bile salts, say they emulsify fat. Explain that this gives a larger surface area for lipase, so fat is digested faster. Do not say bile digests fat or breaks it into fatty acids, because that is lipase, and do not confuse bile salts with bile pigments, which are wastes.

questions.prompt: Write the dental formula of an adult human and state the role of incisors and molars.
questions.model: The adult human dental formula is 2.1.2.3 over 2.1.2.3, giving 32 teeth in total. Incisors are chisel-shaped with sharp, flat edges and are used for biting and cutting food. Molars are broad with ridged cusps and are used for crushing and grinding food.

questions.prompt: What is peristalsis? Describe how it moves food along the gut and explain why dietary fibre helps it.
questions.model: Peristalsis is a wave of muscular contraction that passes along the wall of the gut. The circular muscle just behind the bolus contracts, narrowing the gut and squeezing the food forwards, while the circular muscle just in front relaxes to widen the gut and receive it; the wave then moves along. Dietary fibre adds bulk that the gut muscles can grip and push against, so peristalsis stays effective and constipation is prevented.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between mechanical and chemical digestion. Describe the mechanical breakdown of food in the stomach and in the duodenum.
questions.model: Mechanical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, or fat into smaller droplets, without changing the molecules or breaking bonds; chemical digestion breaks bonds by hydrolysis using enzymes. In the stomach, the three layers of smooth muscle churn the food with gastric juice into chyme, and the pyloric sphincter releases small amounts of chyme into the duodenum at a time. In the duodenum, bile salts emulsify fat: they coat the fat droplets and break them into many tiny droplets, which increases the surface area for lipase. No bonds are broken in emulsification. Bile itself contains no enzymes.
